Optimal Matching between Point Clouds

This opening chapter isolates the simplest form of optimal transport: pairing two finite, equally weighted point clouds of the same cardinality. The stakes are algorithmic and geometric at once: one sees the combinatorial nature of transport, the special simplicity of the line, and the limitations of permutations once cardinalities or weights differ. Classical assignment algorithms such as the Hungarian and auction methods Kuhn, 1955Bertsekas, 1992 provide the computational backdrop, while the restriction to equal cardinalities and weights motivates the Kantorovich relaxation.

Monge Problem for Discrete Points¶

This section formulates matching as Monge’s deterministic transport problem on two equally weighted clouds. The one-dimensional case is a transparent reference case where the optimal map can be read off by sorting.

Assignment Problem¶

Let C∈Rn×n\C\in\RR^{n\times n}C∈Rn×n be a cost matrix, where Ci,j\C_{i,j}Ci,j​ is the cost of pairing source iii with target jjj, and let Perm(n)\Perm(n)Perm(n) denote the bijections of {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}{1,…,n}. The optimal assignment problem is

min⁡σ∈Perm(n)1n∑i=1nCi,σ(i).\min_{\sigma \in \Perm(n)} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \C_{i,\sigma(i)}.σ∈Perm(n)min​n1​i=1∑n​Ci,σ(i)​.
(1)

When Ci,j=c(xi,yj)\C_{i,j}=c(x_i,y_j)Ci,j​=c(xi​,yj​), this is the Monge problem between the two uniform empirical measures. The factor 1/n1/n1/n records the mass of each atom but does not change the optimizer. Exhaustive search evaluates all n!n!n! permutations and is therefore impractical. Without additional assumptions on C\CC, the optimizer need not be unique.

Convex Costs on the Line¶

In one dimension, convex costs select monotone matchings.

Proposition: Monotone Matching on the Line

Assume that the source points are pairwise distinct and that the target points are pairwise distinct. If Ci,j=h(xi−yj)\C_{i,j}=h(x_i-y_j)Ci,j​=h(xi​−yj​) for a strictly convex function h:R→Rh:\RR\to\RRh:R→R, then the unique optimizer is the order-preserving permutation, characterized by

(xi−xi′)(yσ(i)−yσ(i′))>0for every i≠i′.(x_i-x_{i'})(y_{\sigma(i)}-y_{\sigma(i')}) > 0 \qquad\text{for every }i\neq i'.(xi​−xi′​)(yσ(i)​−yσ(i′)​)>0for every i=i′.
(2)
Proof

An assignment that does not preserve order contains an inversion: after relabeling, x<x′x<x'x<x′ are matched to y′>yy'>yy′>y. Set d=y′−y>0d=y'-y>0d=y′−y>0 and

D(s)=h(s)−h(s−d)d.D(s)=\frac{h(s)-h(s-d)}{d}.D(s)=dh(s)−h(s−d)​.
(3)

Strict convexity makes DDD strictly increasing. Therefore

h(x−y′)+h(x′−y)−h(x−y)−h(x′−y′)=d(D(x′−y)−D(x−y)). h(x-y')+h(x'-y)-h(x-y)-h(x'-y') =d\bigl(D(x'-y)-D(x-y)\bigr).h(x−y′)+h(x′−y)−h(x−y)−h(x′−y′)=d(D(x′−y)−D(x−y)).
(4)

This quantity is positive because x−y<x′−yx-y<x'-yx−y<x′−y. Swapping the inverted targets strictly lowers the cost. Repeating the exchange eliminates every inversion; the only order-preserving bijection between the sorted clouds pairs equal ranks.

For convex but not strictly convex hhh, the same exchange inequality is non-strict. Equal-rank matching remains optimal, but other optimizers may coexist. Choose sorting permutations σX,σY\sigma_X,\sigma_YσX​,σY​ such that

xσX(1)≤xσX(2)≤⋯andyσY(1)≤yσY(2)≤⋯ ,x_{\sigma_X(1)} \leq x_{\sigma_X(2)} \leq \cdots \qquad\text{and}\qquad y_{\sigma_Y(1)} \leq y_{\sigma_Y(2)} \leq \cdots,xσX​(1)​≤xσX​(2)​≤⋯andyσY​(1)​≤yσY​(2)​≤⋯,
(5)

and then map xσX(k)x_{\sigma_X(k)}xσX​(k)​ to yσY(k)y_{\sigma_Y(k)}yσY​(k)​. Equivalently, an optimal transport is σ=σY∘σX−1\sigma=\sigma_Y\circ\sigma_X^{-1}σ=σY​∘σX−1​. Comparison sorting costs O(nlog⁡n)O(n\log n)O(nlogn) in the worst case with mergesort or heapsort; quicksort has this complexity only in expectation.

Concave Costs on the Line¶

Concavity reverses the exchange preference: one long and one short displacement can cost less than two displacements of intermediate length. Thus costs c(x,y)=g(∣x−y∣)c(x,y)=g(|x-y|)c(x,y)=g(∣x−y∣) with ggg strictly concave and nondecreasing, such as g(r)=rpg(r)=r^pg(r)=rp for 0<p<10<p<10<p<1, favor nested or crossing assignments rather than equal ranks. This is the regime studied by Gangbo and McCann Gangbo & McCann, 1996.

For a source point, its right neighbor is the nearest target to its right such that the intervening open interval contains equally many sources and targets; left neighbors and target-to-source neighbors are defined symmetrically. Iterating this balanced-neighbor relation partitions a unit-mass problem into independent alternating chains. On a chain

p1<q1<p2<q2<⋯<pN<qN,p_1<q_1<p_2<q_2<\cdots<p_N<q_N,p1​<q1​<p2​<q2​<⋯<pN​<qN​,
(6)

with the opposite orientation handled by exchanging ppp and qqq, the local indicators are

Ikp(i)=c(pi,qi+k)+∑r=0k−1c(pi+r+1,qi+r)−∑r=0kc(pi+r,qi+r),I_k^p(i) =c(p_i,q_{i+k}) +\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}c(p_{i+r+1},q_{i+r}) -\sum_{r=0}^{k}c(p_{i+r},q_{i+r}),Ikp​(i)=c(pi​,qi+k​)+r=0∑k−1​c(pi+r+1​,qi+r​)−r=0∑k​c(pi+r​,qi+r​),
(7)

and

Ikq(i)=c(pi+k+1,qi)+∑r=1kc(pi+r,qi+r)−∑r=0kc(pi+r+1,qi+r).I_k^q(i) =c(p_{i+k+1},q_i) +\sum_{r=1}^{k}c(p_{i+r},q_{i+r}) -\sum_{r=0}^{k}c(p_{i+r+1},q_{i+r}).Ikq​(i)=c(pi+k+1​,qi​)+r=1∑k​c(pi+r​,qi+r​)−r=0∑k​c(pi+r+1​,qi+r​).
(8)

After the relevant lower-order indicators have been found nonnegative, a negative Ikp(i)I_k^p(i)Ikp​(i) certifies pi+r↔qi+r−1p_{i+r}\leftrightarrow q_{i+r-1}pi+r​↔qi+r−1​, while a negative Ikq(i)I_k^q(i)Ikq​(i) certifies pi+r↔qi+rp_{i+r}\leftrightarrow q_{i+r}pi+r​↔qi+r​, for r=1,…,kr=1,\ldots,kr=1,…,k. Recursively removing certified blocks gives an exact O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) algorithm for equal unit masses; the extension to arbitrary real masses has a larger O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) worst-case bound Delon et al., 2012. Repeatedly matching the closest red-blue pair is a simpler heuristic, with quantitative guarantees for g(r)=rpg(r)=r^pg(r)=rp when 0<p<1/20<p<1/20<p<1/2 Ottolini & Steinerberger, 2025.

Histogram Equalization¶

If ϕ:R→R\phi:\RR\to\RRϕ:R→R is strictly increasing and h:R+→Rh:\RR_+\to\RRh:R+​→R is convex and nondecreasing, sorting also solves the problem with cost h(∣ϕ(x)−ϕ(y)∣)h(|\phi(x)-\phi(y)|)h(∣ϕ(x)−ϕ(y)∣). A typical application is grayscale histogram equalization. For equal-size samples with distinct ranks, monotone rearrangement gives the exact assignment to a prescribed target histogram. Repeated intensities require consistent tie-breaking or mass splitting, but the quantile construction remains canonical. It matches intensity distributions rather than spatial pixel locations.

Figure Div applies this construction to image intensities and shows simultaneously the interpolated images and the monotone evolution of their histograms.

show_book_figure("monge-histogram-equalization")

Histogram equalization as one-dimensional Monge transport on pixel intensities. The map is the monotone rearrangement T=Qβ∘FαT=Q_\beta\circ F_\alphaT=Qβ​∘Fα​; here β\betaβ is a truncated Gaussian concentrated near dark intensities. The images are interpolated pointwise by It=(1−t)I+tT(I)I_t=(1-t)I+tT(I)It​=(1−t)I+tT(I), and all histograms share the same vertical scale.

The interactive view below exposes the target mean, target standard deviation, and interpolation time.

target_mean = 0.18
target_sigma = 0.105
interpolation = 0.67  # 0 is the original image, 1 is fully equalized
fig = plot_histogram_equalization(
    target_mean=target_mean,
    target_sigma=target_sigma,
    interpolation=interpolation,
)

Interactive panel. Use the mean, standard-deviation, and time sliders to move the target intensity law and follow the resulting image equalization and histogram deformation.

Flat Directions for the Linear Cost¶

Strict convexity makes every optimizer increasing and, for distinct points, unique. For a merely convex cost such as ∣x−y∣|x-y|∣x−y∣, non-increasing optimal assignments can coexist. The next example exhibits a genuine flat direction of the linear cost.

Example: Discrete book-shifting and non-uniqueness for W1\Wass_1W1​

Fix m≥1m\geq1m≥1 and consider two equal-cardinality point clouds

X={1,…,2m},Y={m+1,…,3m},X=\{1,\ldots,2m\}, \qquad Y=\{m+1,\ldots,3m\},X={1,…,2m},Y={m+1,…,3m},
(9)

with uniform weights. The monotone assignment sends iii to i+mi+mi+m and has average cost mmm for c(x,y)=∣x−y∣c(x,y)=|x-y|c(x,y)=∣x−y∣. It is not unique. The discrete book-shifting assignment

Tbook(i)={i+2m,1≤i≤m,i,m<i≤2m,T_{\rm book}(i)= \begin{cases} i+2m, & 1\leq i\leq m,\\ i, & m<i\leq 2m, \end{cases}Tbook​(i)={i+2m,i,​1≤i≤m,m<i≤2m,​
(10)

is also a bijection from XXX to YYY and has the same average cost:

12m∑i=12m∣Tbook(i)−i∣=12m∑i=1m2m=m.\frac1{2m}\sum_{i=1}^{2m}|T_{\rm book}(i)-i| = \frac1{2m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}2m =m.2m1​i=1∑2m​∣Tbook​(i)−i∣=2m1​i=1∑m​2m=m.
(11)

Optimality follows from the lower bound

12m∑i=12m∣yσ(i)−i∣≥12m∑i=12m(yσ(i)−i)=m,\frac1{2m}\sum_{i=1}^{2m}|y_{\sigma(i)}-i| \geq \frac1{2m}\sum_{i=1}^{2m}(y_{\sigma(i)}-i) =m,2m1​i=1∑2m​∣yσ(i)​−i∣≥2m1​i=1∑2m​(yσ(i)​−i)=m,
(12)

which holds for every assignment because the target sum is fixed. The continuous Monge version of the same book-shifting phenomenon is given later in Example Example: Book-shifting in the Monge problem.

For ∣x−y∣p|x-y|^p∣x−y∣p with p>1p>1p>1, this degeneracy disappears: the monotone assignment has average cost mpm^pmp, whereas the book-shifting assignment has average cost 2p−1mp>mp2^{p-1}m^p>m^p2p−1mp>mp. Strict convexity penalizes concentrating all displacement on half of the points.

Optimal Transport on the Circle¶

The sorting rule on the line has a periodic analogue. Identify the circle with S1=R/Z\mathbb S^1=\RR/\mathbb ZS1=R/Z, let

dS1(x,y):=min⁡k∈Z∣x−y+k∣,cp(x,y):=dS1(x,y)p,p>1.d_{\mathbb S^1}(x,y):=\min_{k\in\mathbb Z}|x-y+k|, \qquad c_p(x,y):=d_{\mathbb S^1}(x,y)^p, \qquad p>1.dS1​(x,y):=k∈Zmin​∣x−y+k∣,cp​(x,y):=dS1​(x,y)p,p>1.
(13)

The only extra datum, compared with the line, is where one opens the circle. Once a cut has been chosen, the circle is unfolded into an interval and the one-dimensional monotone assignment can be used. In the discrete case, changing the cut is the same as applying a cyclic shift to one of the two circular orderings.

Proposition: Discrete Circle Transport by a Cut

Assume that the 2n2n2n points x1,…,xn,y1,…,ynx_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_nx1​,…,xn​,y1​,…,yn​ are pairwise distinct. Let x(1),…,x(n)x_{(1)},\ldots,x_{(n)}x(1)​,…,x(n)​ and y(1),…,y(n)y_{(1)},\ldots,y_{(n)}y(1)​,…,y(n)​ denote fixed cyclic orderings, with indices understood modulo nnn. For the cost cpc_pcp​, p>1p>1p>1, every optimal assignment is a cyclic shift

x(k)⟼y(k+s),k∈{1,…,n},s∈{0,…,n−1},x_{(k)} \longmapsto y_{(k+s)}, \qquad k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, \qquad s\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\},x(k)​⟼y(k+s)​,k∈{1,…,n},s∈{0,…,n−1},
(14)

and its cost is obtained by minimizing

1n∑k=1ndS1 ⁣(x(k),y(k+s))p\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n d_{\mathbb S^1}\!\left(x_{(k)},y_{(k+s)}\right)^pn1​k=1∑n​dS1​(x(k)​,y(k+s)​)p
(15)

over the nnn possible shifts. For each optimal assignment, one can choose a cut θ∈S1∖({xi}i∪{yj}j)\theta\in\mathbb S^1\setminus(\{x_i\}_i\cup\{y_j\}_j)θ∈S1∖({xi​}i​∪{yj​}j​) crossed by none of its shortest transport arcs. After lifting the points to (θ,θ+1)(\theta,\theta+1)(θ,θ+1), the assignment is the equal-rank monotone matching on this interval.

Proof

Fix an optimal assignment and let γi\gamma_iγi​ be an open shortest arc from xix_ixi​ to its matched target, choosing either orientation for an antipodal pair. The path-uncrossing lemma of Delon, Rabin, and Gousseau says that if two arcs of an optimal assignment intersect, then they have the same orientation and neither is strictly contained in the other Rabin et al., 2011. Indeed, opposite orientations or strict containment would allow a two-edge exchange that is strictly cheaper by monotonicity and strict convexity of r↦rpr\mapsto r^pr↦rp.

Suppose that the arcs cover the circle. Because they are open, every source lies in another transport arc. Ordering the sources cyclically and applying the path-uncrossing lemma propagates a common orientation: either each forward neighbor lies in the preceding arc, or the analogous statement holds backward. Cyclically reassigning the targets in that orientation then shortens every arc, contradicting optimality. Hence a point θ\thetaθ lies outside their union.

Cut at θ\thetaθ and lift the circle to (θ,θ+1)(\theta,\theta+1)(θ,θ+1). Each matched geodesic avoids the cut, so its circular length is the ordinary distance between its lifted endpoints. The monotone matching proposition on the line implies that the lifted assignment preserves order. An order-preserving bijection between two cyclically ordered finite sets is a cyclic shift. Minimizing over the nnn shifts therefore recovers the optimum. The argument and its extensions to convex costs and nonuniform masses are developed in Rabin et al., 2011Delon et al., 2010.

Two-Dimensional Assignments¶

Sorting no longer orders a planar cloud, but a simple local exchange still rules out proper crossings for the Euclidean-distance cost. This observation, already present in Monge’s geometric reasoning, is necessary but far from sufficient for computing an optimum.

Proposition: No Proper Crossings in Euclidean-Distance Matchings

Let x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn∈R2x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\RR^2x1​,…,xn​,y1​,…,yn​∈R2 and let c(x,y)=∥x−y∥c(x,y)=\norm{x-y}c(x,y)=∥x−y∥. If σ\sigmaσ is optimal, then two matched segments cannot cross properly: their relative interiors cannot meet at a point where their supporting lines are distinct.

Proof

Suppose that [xi,yσ(i)][x_i,y_{\sigma(i)}][xi​,yσ(i)​] and [xj,yσ(j)][x_j,y_{\sigma(j)}][xj​,yσ(j)​] cross properly at zzz. The triangle inequality along the two reconnected paths gives

∥xi−yσ(j)∥≤∥xi−z∥+∥z−yσ(j)∥,\norm{x_i-y_{\sigma(j)}} \leq \norm{x_i-z}+\norm{z-y_{\sigma(j)}},∥∥​xi​−yσ(j)​∥∥​≤∥xi​−z∥+∥∥​z−yσ(j)​∥∥​,
(16)

and the analogous inequality after exchanging iii and jjj. The sum of the right-hand sides is the cost of the two original segments. At least one inequality is strict because the crossing is non-collinear. Swapping the two targets therefore strictly decreases the cost, a contradiction. Collinear overlaps are excluded because the exchange can then have equal cost.

This property alone is not enough to lead to an efficient algorithm. Non-crossing is only a necessary local test, not a compact certificate of optimality. For instance, if nnn sources and nnn targets are placed alternately on the boundary of a convex polygon, the number of non-crossing perfect matchings is the Catalan number

Cn=1n+1(2nn)∼4nπn3/2.C_n=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n} \sim \frac{4^n}{\sqrt{\pi}n^{3/2}}.Cn​=n+11​(n2n​)∼π​n3/24n​.
(17)
Remark: Catalan count of alternating non-crossing matchings

The count follows from the standard Catalan recurrence. Fix one red vertex rrr. In a non-crossing perfect matching, if rrr is matched to a blue vertex bbb, the chord [r,b][r,b][r,b] splits the polygon into two smaller polygons. Since the boundary colors alternate, each side contains the same number of red and blue vertices. If one side contains kkk red and kkk blue vertices, the other contains n−1−kn-1-kn−1−k red and n−1−kn-1-kn−1−k blue vertices. Non-crossing matchings on the two sides are independent, because no segment can cross the chord [r,b][r,b][r,b]. Thus, denoting by MnM_nMn​ the number of such matchings, one has

M0=1,Mn=∑k=0n−1MkMn−1−k.M_0=1, \qquad M_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} M_k M_{n-1-k}.M0​=1,Mn​=k=0∑n−1​Mk​Mn−1−k​.
(18)

This recurrence characterizes the Catalan numbers, hence Mn=CnM_n=C_nMn​=Cn​.

Thus even after forbidding proper crossings, exhaustive search remains exponential. The two-segment swap explains why a transverse crossing cannot be optimal, but it does not select among the exponentially many planar matchings that survive this local test.

Input: Equal-weight point clouds (xi)i=1n(x_i)_{i=1}^n(xi​)i=1n​, (yj)j=1n(y_j)_{j=1}^n(yj​)j=1n​ on R\RRR; convex cost h(x−y)h(x-y)h(x−y).

Output: Optimal permutation σ\sigmaσ.

Sort source and target points: xσX(1)≤⋯≤xσX(n),yσY(1)≤⋯≤yσY(n).x_{\sigma_X(1)}\leq\cdots\leq x_{\sigma_X(n)}, \qquad y_{\sigma_Y(1)}\leq\cdots\leq y_{\sigma_Y(n)}.xσX​(1)​≤⋯≤xσX​(n)​,yσY​(1)​≤⋯≤yσY​(n)​.

For k=1,…,nk=1,\ldots,nk=1,…,n do:

Match xσX(k)x_{\sigma_X(k)}xσX​(k)​ with yσY(k)y_{\sigma_Y(k)}yσY​(k)​.

Return σ=σY∘σX−1.\sigma=\sigma_Y\circ\sigma_X^{-1}.σ=σY​∘σX−1​.

Algorithm: Concave line matching by local indicators

Input: Two nnn-point unit-mass clouds on R\RRR; cost c(x,y)=g(∣x−y∣)c(x,y)=g(|x-y|)c(x,y)=g(∣x−y∣) with ggg strictly concave and nondecreasing.

Output: Optimal concave-cost matching MMM.

Sort combined red-blue sequence on the line.

Construct the independent alternating chains induced by the balanced-neighbor relation.

Initialize: Set M=∅M=\emptysetM=∅.

While an active chain remains do:

Select the leftmost active chain and set the indicator order k=1k=1k=1.

While the chain is nonempty do:

Retrieve or compute all admissible order-kkk indicators Ikp(i)I_k^p(i)Ikp​(i) and Ikq(i)I_k^q(i)Ikq​(i).

If a negative indicator is found then:

Select the negative indicator with smallest site index iii; prefer Ikp(i)I_k^p(i)Ikp​(i) to break a tie.

Add its certified block of kkk neighboring pairs to MMM.

Remove their endpoints, invalidate affected cached indicators, relabel the chains, and set k=1k=1k=1.

Else if kkk is below the maximal admissible order then set k←k+1k\leftarrow k+1k←k+1.

Else match the remaining chain by equal indices in its current orientation and remove it.

Return MMM.

After sorting, direct enumeration costs O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2). Faster methods exploit the convex dependence of the circular transport cost on a continuous shift parameter for weighted histograms Delon et al., 2010.

Hungarian Algorithm¶

We now present a first algorithm for solving the optimal matching problem. The Hungarian method Kuhn, 1955Burkard et al., 2009 provides a gentle, self-contained preview of duality: it computes a permutation together with a certificate of its optimality. The auction algorithm Bertsekas, 1981Bertsekas, 1992 is postponed to Section Auction Algorithm, after discrete duality and the semi-dual formulation have been fully developed.

Hungarian Primal-Dual Method¶

The method constructs an assignment and its optimality certificate simultaneously. Its derivation below uses only the elementary lower bound derived next; Section Discrete Dual later embeds this certificate in general discrete Kantorovich duality.

The factor 1/n1/n1/n in the assignment objective does not affect its optimizer, so consider the unnormalized dual problem

max⁡(f,g)∈Rn×Rn∑i=1nfi+∑j=1ngjsubject tofi+gj≤Ci,j∀i,j.\max_{(\fD,\gD)\in\RR^n\times\RR^n} \sum_{i=1}^n\fD_i+\sum_{j=1}^n\gD_j \qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \fD_i+\gD_j\leq\C_{i,j}\quad\forall i,j.(f,g)∈Rn×Rnmax​i=1∑n​fi​+j=1∑n​gj​subject tofi​+gj​≤Ci,j​∀i,j.
(19)

The certificate used by both Hungarian and auction methods is worth isolating.

Proposition: Dual Certificate for an Assignment

Let (f,g)(\fD,\gD)(f,g) be feasible for the assignment dual. Then every τ∈Perm(n)\tau\in\Perm(n)τ∈Perm(n) satisfies

∑iCi,τ(i)≥∑ifi+∑jgj.\sum_i\C_{i,\tau(i)} \geq\sum_i\fD_i+\sum_j\gD_j.i∑​Ci,τ(i)​≥i∑​fi​+j∑​gj​.
(20)

If a permutation σ\sigmaσ uses only tight constraints,

fi+gσ(i)=Ci,σ(i)for every i,\fD_i+\gD_{\sigma(i)}=\C_{i,\sigma(i)} \qquad\text{for every }i,fi​+gσ(i)​=Ci,σ(i)​for every i,
(21)

then σ\sigmaσ is an optimal assignment and (f,g)(\fD,\gD)(f,g) is dual optimal. Equality in the lower bound at τ=σ\tau=\sigmaτ=σ holds if and only if every edge (i,σ(i))(i,\sigma(i))(i,σ(i)) is tight.

Proof

Dual feasibility gives Ci,τ(i)≥fi+gτ(i)\C_{i,\tau(i)}\geq\fD_i+\gD_{\tau(i)}Ci,τ(i)​≥fi​+gτ(i)​ for every iii. Summing and using that τ\tauτ permutes the target indices yields

∑iCi,τ(i)≥∑ifi+∑igτ(i)=∑ifi+∑jgj.\sum_i\C_{i,\tau(i)} \geq \sum_i\fD_i+\sum_i\gD_{\tau(i)} = \sum_i\fD_i+\sum_j\gD_j.i∑​Ci,τ(i)​≥i∑​fi​+i∑​gτ(i)​=i∑​fi​+j∑​gj​.
(22)

If all edges selected by σ\sigmaσ are tight, its assignment cost equals the dual value of (f,g)(\fD,\gD)(f,g). The lower bound shows that no permutation has smaller cost. Applied to σ\sigmaσ and any other feasible dual pair, it also shows that no feasible dual value can exceed this cost. Conversely, the difference is the sum of the nonnegative slacks Ci,σ(i)−fi−gσ(i)\C_{i,\sigma(i)}-\fD_i-\gD_{\sigma(i)}Ci,σ(i)​−fi​−gσ(i)​, and it vanishes exactly when every one of these slacks vanishes.

This is exactly the uniform-mass specialization of the discrete Kantorovich dual (2), multiplied by nnn.

The method maintains feasible potentials and a partial matching MMM, meaning a set of source--target pairs in which no vertex occurs twice. Its slack, or reduced cost, is

si,j=Ci,j−fi−gj≥0.s_{i,j}=\C_{i,j}-\fD_i-\gD_j\geq0.si,j​=Ci,j​−fi​−gj​≥0.
(23)

The equality graph consists precisely of the zero-slack edges,

E(f,g)={(i,j):si,j=0}={(i,j):fi+gj=Ci,j}.E(\fD,\gD)=\{(i,j):s_{i,j}=0\} =\{(i,j):\fD_i+\gD_j=\C_{i,j}\}.E(f,g)={(i,j):si,j​=0}={(i,j):fi​+gj​=Ci,j​}.
(24)

The invariant M⊂E(f,g)M\subset E(\fD,\gD)M⊂E(f,g) means that every matched pair already saturates its dual constraint. If MMM is perfect, Proposition Proposition: Dual Certificate for an Assignment certifies that its associated permutation is optimal. It remains to enlarge MMM while preserving dual feasibility and M⊂E(f,g)M\subset E(\fD,\gD)M⊂E(f,g).

To increase the matching, choose an unmatched source i0i_0i0​. Starting from that root, grow a tree in the bipartite equality graph. From a reached source, follow a zero-slack edge to a new target; from a reached target that is already matched, follow its unique matched edge back to a source. The tree edges therefore alternate between unmatched and matched edges, which explains the term alternating tree. Write p(j)p(j)p(j) for the source preceding a reached target jjj, and q(i)q(i)q(i) for the matched target preceding a reached non-root source iii. If the tree reaches an unmatched target, these pointers form an augmenting path. Exchanging matched and unmatched edges along this path increases ∣M∣|M|∣M∣ by one.

Let SSS and TTT denote the reached source and target sets, and let NE(S)={j:∃i∈S, (i,j)∈E(f,g)}N_E(S)=\{j:\exists i\in S,\ (i,j)\in E(\fD,\gD)\}NE​(S)={j:∃i∈S, (i,j)∈E(f,g)}. If no equality edge leaves SSS toward an unreached target, shift the potentials by the smallest such slack:

δ=min⁡i∈S, j∉T(Ci,j−fi−gj),fi←fi+δ (i∈S),gj←gj−δ (j∈T).\delta=\min_{i\in S,\ j\notin T} \bigl(\C_{i,j}-\fD_i-\gD_j\bigr), \qquad \fD_i\leftarrow\fD_i+\delta\ (i\in S), \qquad \gD_j\leftarrow\gD_j-\delta\ (j\in T).δ=i∈S, j∈/Tmin​(Ci,j​−fi​−gj​),fi​←fi​+δ (i∈S),gj​←gj​−δ (j∈T).
(25)

Here δ>0\delta>0δ>0 because no edge from SSS to TcT^cTc is currently tight. The update leaves slacks unchanged on S×TS\times TS×T, decreases them by δ\deltaδ on S×TcS\times T^cS×Tc, and increases them on Sc×TS^c\times TSc×T. Feasibility and existing tree edges are preserved, while at least one new equality edge appears from SSS to TcT^cTc. Since ∣S∣=∣T∣+1|S|=|T|+1∣S∣=∣T∣+1 before a free target is reached, the dual objective increases by δ(∣S∣−∣T∣)=δ\delta(|S|-|T|)=\deltaδ(∣S∣−∣T∣)=δ.

A cubic implementation stores, for every unreached target,

ℓj=min⁡i∈Ssi,j\ell_j=\min_{i\in S}s_{i,j}ℓj​=i∈Smin​si,j​
(26)

and a parent source p(j)p(j)p(j) attaining the minimum. When a source i′i'i′ enters SSS, each unreached target is updated by comparing ℓj\ell_jℓj​ with the single new slack si′,js_{i',j}si′,j​. A dual shift uses δ=min⁡j∉Tℓj\delta=\min_{j\notin T}\ell_jδ=minj∈/T​ℓj​ and replaces ℓj\ell_jℓj​ by ℓj−δ\ell_j-\deltaℓj​−δ for j∉Tj\notin Tj∈/T. A tree expansion therefore costs O(n)O(n)O(n) rather than requiring a rescan of S×TcS\times T^cS×Tc.

Hungarian and auction methods use the same dual potentials and reduced costs in different ways. Hungarian grows an exact zero-slack augmenting tree, whereas the auction method in Section Auction Algorithm uses ϵ\epsilonϵ-relaxed contacts, price bids, and ownership changes. Proposition: Correctness and Complexity of the Hungarian Primal-Dual Method

For every cost matrix C∈Rn×n\C\in\RR^{n\times n}C∈Rn×n, the Hungarian algorithm terminates after nnn augmentation phases. It returns a permutation σ∈Perm(n)\sigma\in\Perm(n)σ∈Perm(n) and feasible potentials (f,g)(\fD,\gD)(f,g) satisfying

fi+gσ(i)=Ci,σ(i)∀i.\fD_i+\gD_{\sigma(i)}=\C_{i,\sigma(i)} \qquad\forall i.fi​+gσ(i)​=Ci,σ(i)​∀i.
(27)

Consequently, σ\sigmaσ is optimal. With the maintained slacks (26), the algorithm uses O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) arithmetic and comparison operations and O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) storage, including the cost matrix.

Proof

Initialization is dual feasible and the empty matching lies in the equality graph. At the beginning of a phase, the slack initialization gives

ℓj=min⁡i∈Ssi,j=sp(j),j(j∉T).\ell_j=\min_{i\in S}s_{i,j}=s_{p(j),j} \qquad(j\notin T).ℓj​=i∈Smin​si,j​=sp(j),j​(j∈/T).
(28)

This identity is preserved when a matched source i′i'i′ enters SSS, because the algorithm compares every ℓj\ell_jℓj​ with the single new candidate si′,js_{i',j}si′,j​.

Before a free target is reached, every target in TTT is matched to a source in SSS, while every source in SSS except the unmatched root was reached through its matched target. Thus ∣S∣=∣T∣+1|S|=|T|+1∣S∣=∣T∣+1, so TTT cannot contain every target. Dual feasibility gives

δ=min⁡j∉Tℓj=min⁡i∈S, j∉Tsi,j≥0.\delta=\min_{j\notin T}\ell_j =\min_{i\in S,\,j\notin T}s_{i,j}\geq0.δ=j∈/Tmin​ℓj​=i∈S,j∈/Tmin​si,j​≥0.
(29)

After the potential update,

si,j+={si,j,(i,j)∈S×T,si,j−δ,(i,j)∈S×Tc,si,j+δ,(i,j)∈Sc×T,si,j,(i,j)∈Sc×Tc.s_{i,j}^{+}= \begin{cases} s_{i,j},&(i,j)\in S\times T,\\ s_{i,j}-\delta,&(i,j)\in S\times T^c,\\ s_{i,j}+\delta,&(i,j)\in S^c\times T,\\ s_{i,j},&(i,j)\in S^c\times T^c. \end{cases}si,j+​=⎩⎨⎧​si,j​,si,j​−δ,si,j​+δ,si,j​,​(i,j)∈S×T,(i,j)∈S×Tc,(i,j)∈Sc×T,(i,j)∈Sc×Tc.​
(30)

All slacks remain nonnegative. For j∉Tj\notin Tj∈/T, both the slacks from SSS and ℓj\ell_jℓj​ decrease by δ\deltaδ, so the maintained-minimum identity remains valid. At least one ℓj\ell_jℓj​ becomes zero, and p(j)p(j)p(j) supplies the corresponding equality edge. Every matched edge remains tight.

Each inner iteration adds a new target to TTT. It either reaches a free target or adds that target’s matched source to SSS and updates the slack array. Hence a phase reaches a free target after at most nnn iterations. The pointers ppp and qqq trace an alternating path; flipping it preserves the matching property, increases ∣M∣|M|∣M∣ by one, and uses only equality edges. Starting from the empty matching, exactly nnn phases produce a perfect matching.

At termination every matched edge is tight, so Proposition Proposition: Dual Certificate for an Assignment directly proves that σ\sigmaσ is optimal and the returned potentials are dual optimal. This is the finite assignment instance of the complementary-slackness mechanism proved in general in Proposition Proposition: Discrete Complementary Slackness. Initializing the slack array costs O(n)O(n)O(n). Each inner iteration scans at most nnn targets to find δ\deltaδ, update the slacks, and compare them with one newly reached source row. It therefore costs O(n)O(n)O(n), giving O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) per phase and O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) overall. The cost matrix requires O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) storage, while the matching, reached sets, parent arrays, and slacks require only O(n)O(n)O(n) additional storage.

The chapter has exposed two complementary routes to finite matching: geometry can reduce the problem to sorting, while primal-dual potentials give a global certificate for an arbitrary cost matrix. The next chapter passes from finite permutations to transport maps between general measures.
